judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 20, which would have stopped insurance companies and other businesses from charging extra for a paper bill or notice. They could still have charged for a second copy of a paper document already sent. Breaking the rule would have counted as an unfair trade practice. The state can act on those.The Alaska House passed it 26-14. The Alaska Senate did not vote on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 58, which would have changed who picks the head of the Office of Public Advocacy. That office provides lawyers and court-appointed guardians. It steps in when the Public Defender Agency cannot take a case. The job would have gone to a public advocate named by the governor. The names would have come from the Alaska Judicial Council. The legislature would have had to approve the choice. The term would have been four years. The governor could have removed the person only for good cause, in writing to the legislature. Powers now held by the commissioner of administration would have moved to that officer.The Alaska House passed it 27-12. The Alaska Senate did not vote on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 111, which would have given owners and independent repair shops a right to fix everyday electronics. A maker would have had to hand them the same manuals, parts and tools it gives its own approved repairers. It could not have charged them a higher price. Makers could not have used software that blocks a working replacement part. Nor could they have used software that slows the device when one is fitted. Medical devices, cars, fire alarms and building security systems would not have been covered. Breaking the rules would have counted as an unfair trade practice.The Alaska Senate passed it 15-5. The Alaska House did not vote on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 250, which would have made large data centers pay for the power lines and gas lines built to serve them. Today those costs can be spread across other utility customers. A data center is a building full of computers that store and handle data. The utility and the data center would have signed a contract. The state regulator would have had to approve it. The data center would have had to post security if the utility spent more than $1 million. The contract would have held backup power from fossil fuels to emergencies and testing. The data center would also have had to make a deal with the city or borough. That deal would have covered waste heat, water use and broadband. It would also have had to file a plan for taking the site apart at the end of its life.The Alaska Senate passed it 14-5. The Alaska House did not vote on it, so it did not become law.
